summary: A regenerative approach used alongside other treatments for skin and scalp concerns.
leadAnswer: Exosome therapy applies preparations of exosomes, tiny cell-derived vesicles that carry signalling molecules, to the skin or scalp. At Kaiteki it is usually used alongside another procedure such as microneedling, a laser or PRP, not on its own. The evidence base is still developing, so a doctor assesses whether it suits your plan.

sessionSteps.title: Consultation and assessment
sessionSteps.body: Your first visit is a consultation, not a treatment. A doctor assesses your skin or scalp and decides whether exosome therapy is appropriate, and what it would be combined with.

sessionSteps.title: The accompanying procedure
sessionSteps.body: The session is built around the procedure exosome therapy accompanies: microneedling, a laser, or PRP (platelet-rich plasma).

sessionSteps.title: Application
sessionSteps.body: The exosome preparation is applied to the treated skin or scalp.

sessionSteps.title: Afterwards
sessionSteps.body: You are given aftercare for the combined procedure. A short course spaced a few weeks apart is common, planned for you rather than sold as a package.

afterSession.intro: Downtime is set mostly by the procedure exosome therapy is combined with.

bands.title: The first few days
bands.body: When paired with microneedling or a laser, temporary redness, mild swelling or sensitivity can occur, and typically settles over the following days.

bands.title: Across a course
bands.body: Any change develops gradually across the course, not on the day.

afterSession.aftercare: Gentle skincare and sun protection are usually advised afterwards. Your doctor will give aftercare guidance specific to your treatment.

risks.intro: The doctor explains these, and those of the procedure it accompanies, before you decide.
risks.common: Redness, swelling, sensitivity or irritation at the treated area.
risks.lessCommon: Any procedure it is combined with, such as microneedling, a laser or PRP, carries its own considerations, which are explained alongside it.

It is not established in the way the procedures it accompanies are. The evidence base is still developing.

sections.heading: What is exosome therapy?
body: Exosomes are tiny cell-derived vesicles that carry signalling molecules such as proteins, lipids and RNA. In the body they act as messengers between cells, and this signalling role is why they are being explored in regenerative aesthetics.
Exosome therapy applies preparations of these vesicles to the skin or scalp, usually as part of a wider treatment plan rather than on its own. It is an emerging area of aesthetic medicine.

sections.heading: Why is exosome therapy applied after another procedure?
body: The aim of exosome therapy is to support the skin's or scalp's own repair and renewal processes by delivering exosome-based signalling molecules to the treated area. Because exosomes are small, they are commonly applied after a procedure that briefly opens channels in the skin, such as microneedling or certain lasers.
That is why its role, and its downtime, depend on the procedure it follows.

faqs.a: Common effects are temporary redness, swelling, sensitivity or irritation, and the accompanying procedure carries its own risks. It is an emerging treatment with a developing evidence base, so the doctor sets out what is and is not known before you decide.

faqs.q: Can exosome therapy be combined with other treatments?
faqs.a: Yes, and it usually is: it is commonly applied after microneedling or certain lasers, which briefly open channels in the skin, or alongside PRP.

faqs.q: Who is a suitable candidate for exosome therapy?
faqs.a: People already planning microneedling, a laser or PRP for skin recovery or scalp concerns may be assessed for it. It is deferred in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and certain skin or scalp conditions can rule it out.

faqs.q: When might I notice a change?
faqs.a: Any change develops gradually over the weeks after treatment, not immediately, and the extent varies between people.
